topic: Law of Torts and Consumer Protection: Specific Torts (Focus on Negligence & Donoghue v. Stevenson)
description: This module delves into specific torts, particularly Negligence, Defamation, and Nuisance. It places a special emphasis on the landmark English case of Donoghue v. Stevenson, which revolutionized tort law by establishing the modern concept of negligence and the famous 'Neighbour Principle'.

key_points: Definition: Negligence is the breach of a legal duty to take care, resulting in damage, undesired by the defendant, to the plaintiff.

Three Essential Elements: To succeed in an action for negligence, the plaintiff must prove three things: (1) The defendant owed a legal 'Duty of Care' to the plaintiff; (2) The defendant made a 'Breach' of that duty; (3) The plaintiff suffered 'Damage' as a direct consequence of that breach.

Res Ipsa Loquitur: A legal maxim meaning 'the thing speaks for itself'. In some cases, the plaintiff doesn't need to prove negligence because the circumstances of the accident imply that it could only have happened due to the defendant's negligence.

donoghue_v_stevenson.concept: The Landmark Case: Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932)
key_points: The Facts: Mrs. Donoghue's friend bought her a bottle of ginger beer in a cafe. The bottle was made of dark, opaque glass. After drinking some, she poured the rest, and a decomposed snail fell out. She suffered shock and gastroenteritis.

The Legal Issue: Since Mrs. Donoghue did not buy the drink herself, she had no contract with the cafe owner or the manufacturer (no 'privity of contract'). Previously, one could only sue if they had a direct contract.

The Ruling: The House of Lords ruled in her favor. They established that a manufacturer of products owes a 'duty of care' to the ultimate consumer, regardless of whether a contract exists between them.
The Principle: Formulated by Lord Atkin in the Donoghue case, it answers the question: 'To whom do I owe a duty of care?'
The Rule: 'You must take reasonable care to avoid acts or omissions which you can reasonably foresee would be likely to injure your neighbour.'

Who is a Neighbour?: In law, a neighbour is not just someone who lives next door. It includes 'persons who are so closely and directly affected by my act that I ought reasonably to have them in contemplation as being so affected when I am directing my mind to the acts or omissions which are called in question.'

mcq_bank.subtopic: Donoghue v. Stevenson and Privity of Contract

questions.question: What major legal barrier in tort law was broken by the landmark decision in Donoghue v. Stevenson (1932)?

options.A: It established that only the person who purchased the goods could sue for injuries.
options.B: It ruled that the manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer, eliminating the strict requirement of 'privity of contract' in negligence claims.
options.C: It declared that manufacturers are completely immune from lawsuits if they sell through retailers.
options.D: It established the rule of absolute liability for all food and beverage companies.

questions.explanation: Prior to this case, the doctrine of 'privity of contract' meant only the buyer could sue the seller. Donoghue v. Stevenson established that a manufacturer owes an independent duty of care to the ultimate consumer, regardless of who bought the product.

questions.question: Anil buys a sealed packet of biscuits from a local store and gives it to his sister, Priya. While eating, Priya bites into a piece of metal hidden inside the biscuit and injures her teeth. Based on the precedent of Donoghue v. Stevenson, who can Priya legally sue for negligence?

options.A: She cannot sue anyone because she did not purchase the biscuits herself.
options.B: She can only sue Anil, as he was the one who gave her the biscuits.
options.C: She can sue the manufacturer of the biscuits, because the manufacturer owed a duty of care to her as the ultimate consumer.
options.D: She can only sue the local store owner for selling a defective product.

questions.explanation: Following the exact logic of Donoghue v. Stevenson, the manufacturer owes a duty of care to the ultimate consumer (Priya) to ensure their sealed products are free from harmful defects, even though Priya did not buy the biscuits herself.

questions.question: According to Lord Atkin's 'Neighbour Principle', how does the law determine who your 'neighbour' is in the context of negligence?

options.A: A neighbour is strictly defined as someone who shares a physical property boundary with you.
options.B: A neighbour is anyone who is a citizen of the same country.
options.C: A neighbour is any person whom you can reasonably foresee would be closely and directly affected by your acts or omissions.
options.D: A neighbour is only a person with whom you have signed a formal written contract.

questions.explanation: Lord Atkin defined a 'neighbour' in law not in a geographical sense, but in a conceptual one: anyone who is so closely and directly affected by your actions that you ought reasonably to foresee that your negligence could harm them.
